title: [Chapitre] II. Réalisations topologiques des réseaux : notes manuscrites (06/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Chapter II of the 1986 notes, 'Topological realizations of networks'. The previous page sets up a local notion. For a closed subset A of X, Grothendieck takes a fundamental system of 'conical' neighbourhoods of the point a in X/A, of the form V_t = V_t^0 ⊔ B_t. Their inverse images W_t are neighbourhoods of A with frontier B_t, and X − B_t = W_t^0 ⊔ W_t' (interior plus exterior). This gives a notion of A being 'significatively immersed' in X, with a non-empty 'link' S_A. The previous page then opens a definition of a pair (X,{A,B}), first called a 'cellule topologique', which this page renames 'ficelle' (string).

Definition on this page. A ficelle is a space X with an unordered pair {A,B} of subsets satisfying:
(a) A and B are closed and non-empty;
(b) A ∩ B = ∅;
(c) (X∖A)/B and (X∖B)/A are connected;
(d) A and B are significatively immersed. In particular the realizations of the links are non-empty, S_A ≠ ∅ and S_B ≠ ∅, so A and B are not open.

Left-margin remark. If X = A ∪ B with A, B disjoint and closed, both would be open, contradicting (d). Hence U = X∖(A∪B) is non-empty.

Variant c'. Every connected component U_i of U has a closure that meets both A and B.
- c' ⇒ c: (X∖A)/B is the image of U ∪ {b}, and the closure of each U_i contains b.
- c ⇒ c' when U has finitely many components (e.g. X, A, B tame, 'modérés'). Then each U_i is open. If its closure missed B, U_i would be clopen in X∖A and would disconnect (X∖A)/B.
- Intuitively, A and B are the two ends ('bouts') of the string.

Reduced ficelles. A ficelle is reduced when A and B are points a, b. For any ficelle, collapse A and B separately to get X' = A∖X/B. Then (X,{A,B}) is a ficelle iff (X',{a,b}) is one, since all conditions are local at the ends or concern quotients. NB: a reduced ficelle is connected.

This connectedness claim is genuinely restricted to reduced ficelles. Two disjoint arcs, with A = the two left endpoints and B = the two right endpoints, form a disconnected ficelle whose reduction is a circle.

Lower-left margin. The four conditions are recapitulated, followed by a hereditary remark: removing a suitable closed subset C ⊂ U should leave a ficelle (X∖C, {A,B}).

Purpose. A ficelle is the topological model of an 'edge' (a string with two ends) for realizing combinatorial networks. The next page defines a 'lieu': a closed set C that separates X into a part attached to A and a part attached to B, i.e. a transversal level set of the string.
errors: c' as written in the transcription ('closure contains A and contains B') would be too strong. With it, c ⇒ c' fails even for finitely many components, e.g. two disjoint arcs with A, B each a pair of endpoints. The correct reading (and the one making the stated implications true) is 'rencontre' (meets).
The equivalence c ⇔ c' needs U to have finitely many components, or at least components open in U. Grothendieck states this restriction correctly.

The marginal hereditary claim (X∖C, {A,B}) is a ficelle is only sketched and cannot be true for arbitrary closed C ⊂ U. For instance, C could disconnect U from B, so some hypothesis on C is needed; it is illegible.

ideas.what: Definition of a 'ficelle': a space with two disjoint closed, non-open 'ends' A, B, such that each component of the complement reaches both ends
ideas.modern_name: bipolar space / space with two ends; topological edge, close to a (relative) cobordism between A and B or a two-ended continuum
ideas.usually_credited_to: no single source; related to classical separation theory (Whyburn, Wilder) and to cobordism

ideas.what: Equivalence of the quotient-connectedness condition with 'every component of X∖(A∪B) has closure meeting A and B', under finiteness of components (tame case)
Reduction of a ficelle by collapsing each end to a point; reduced ficelles are connected while general ones need not be
ideas.modern_name: quotient by end sets (collapsing boundary components)

ideas.what: Use of conical/regular neighbourhoods and non-empty links S_A to define 'significant immersion' within a tame-topology framework ('modéré')
ideas.modern_name: regular neighbourhoods / links in PL or o-minimal topology; Grothendieck's 'topologie modérée'
ideas.usually_credited_to: Whitehead, Rourke–Sanderson (PL); van den Dries et al. (o-minimal)
ideas.where_published: tame topology is called for programmatically in Esquisse d'un programme (1984), but not this formalism

missed.claim: Part of a 1986 attempt to build an axiomatic topological theory of realizations of combinatorial 'networks'. The edges are 'ficelles' with ends and transversal 'lieux', grounded in tame-topology notions (links, conical neighbourhoods). This is a concrete fragment of the tame-topology programme announced in the Esquisse, not developed in the literature in this form.
missed.quote: = intuitivement A et B sont les bouts de la ficelle.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only as a historical document of how Grothendieck intended to set up tame topology for graph/map realizations (dessins, networks). The mathematics on this page itself is elementary.

deep.surprise_reason: Careful foundational definitions and elementary point-set lemmas, correct with the right reading of c'. Interesting mainly as evidence of an unpublished 1986 tame-topology formalism for networks, but there is no new theorem here.
transcription_corrections: In c' the verb is 'rencontre B et rencontre A' (meets), not 'contient'. Only this reading makes c' ⇒ c and its converse correct.
The left upper margin reasons that X ≠ A∪B because A and B are not open (they are significatively immersed), so U = X∖(A∪B) is non-empty.
'Cellule topologique' from the previous page is renamed 'ficelle' here: 'Conditions des ficelles' in the margin, 'Fic a)–d)' labels.
